module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 457

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/457](https://www.erdosproblems.com/457)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos457

/--
Is there some $\epsilon > 0$ such that there are infinitely
many $n$ where all primes $p \le (2 + \epsilon) \log n$ divide
$$
  \prod_{1 \le i \le \log n} (n + i)?
$$

This was formalized in Lean by Baretto and van Doorn using Aristotle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Woett/Lean-files/blob/main/ErdosProblem457.lean"]
theorem erdos_457 : answer(True) ↔ ∃ ε > (0 : ℝ),
    { (n : ℕ) | ∀ (p : ℕ), p ≤ (2 + ε) * Real.log n → p.Prime →
      p ∣ ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 ⌊Real.log n⌋₊, (n + i) }.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- Let $q(n, k)$ denote the least prime which does not divide
$\prod_{1 \le i \le k}(n + i)$. -/
noncomputable abbrev q (n : ℕ) (k : ℝ) : ℕ :=
    Nat.find (Nat.exists_prime_not_dvd (n := ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 ⌊k⌋₊, (n + i))
      (Finset.prod_ne_zero_iff.2 fun a ha => by aesop))

/--
More generally, let $q(n, k)$ denote the least prime which
does not divide $\prod_{1 \le i \le k}(n + i)$. This
problem asks whether $q(n, \log n) \ge (2 + \epsilon) \log n$
infinitely often.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_457.variants.qnk : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ ε > (0 : ℝ),
    { (n : ℕ) | (2 + ε) * Real.log n ≤ q n (Real.log n) }.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
Taking $n$ to be the product of primes
between $\log n$ and $(2 + o(1)) \log n$ gives an example where
$$
  q(n, \log n) \ge (2 + o(1)) \log n.
$$
Can one prove that $q(n, \log n) < (1 - \epsilon) (\log n)^2$
for all large $n$ and some $\epsilon > 0$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_457.variants.one_sub : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ ε > (0 : ℝ),
    ∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop, q n (Real.log n) < (1 - ε) * Real.log n ^ 2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos457

status_issues.source_status: Solved affirmatively in March 2026. The cited external proof, describing Kevin Barreto's GPT-5.2 Pro construction and its Aristotle formalization, establishes infinitely many n for which every prime p ≤ 2.1 log n divides the product. Consequently q(n, log n) > 2.1 log n, which proves this variant with ε = 0.1.
status_issues.evidence: The cited Woett/Lean-files/ErdosProblem457.lean contains thm_main and erdos_457 proving the positive lower-bound result. The independent teorth database records problem 457 as “proved (Lean),” updated 2026-03-07; its AI-contributions record dates the result to 2 March 2026. After compatibility-only updates to the cited proof, /workspace/review/ErdosProblem457_transfer.lean derives the exact qnk predicate; #print axioms reports only propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound.
status_issues.suggested_change: Change the category to research solved and replace answer(sorry) with answer(True). The same external proof can support a formal_proof reference, using the equivalence with the main statement.

reformulations.difference: The q formulation uses (2 + ε) log n ≤ q(n, log n), whereas requiring every prime p ≤ (2 + ε) log n to divide the product corresponds pointwise to the strict inequality (2 + ε) log n < q(n, log n). This does not change the existential, infinitely-often problem.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: By Nat.find's specification and minimality, every prime at most a real threshold T divides the product iff T < q. The strict bound immediately implies the weak bound. Conversely, if the weak bound holds infinitely often for ε > 0, discard the finitely many n ≤ 1 and replace ε by ε/2. Since log n > 0 on the remaining set, (2 + ε/2) log n < (2 + ε) log n ≤ q, giving the original divisibility condition infinitely often. This equivalence was proved independently in /workspace/review/scratch.lean as Review457.lower_equivalence, without using any sorry-backed problem theorem.

review.notes: No mathematical misformalizations found. Checked q's existence and minimality, the floor-index convention, empty products, and n = 0 and 1. Small cases were proved in Lean and finite products evaluated. The quadratic upper-bound variant matches Erdős (1979), p. 78; its eventual inequality itself forces ε < 1, so no additional restriction is missing. The main theorem's positive answer and formal_proof record are supported by the independently checked external proof. Direct access to erdosproblems.com/457 and its forum returned Cloudflare 403 responses despite descriptive User-Agent headers, so the primary paper was used for the mathematical comparison. The upper-bound variant's latest status could not be independently confirmed from the live website; no status change is claimed for it. All experiments are under /workspace/review/, and the reviewed file still matches the specified commit.
